title: CAPSUL: A Comprehensive Human Protein Benchmark for Subcellular Localization
one_liner: CAPSUL adds 3D protein shape data to location prediction, letting models learn from structure instead of just sequence.
lead: Where in a cell does a protein end up? This matters for drug design and understanding what proteins do. Before this paper, the only benchmark had protein sequences but not their 3D shapes, even though shapes are central to how proteins work. CAPSUL fixes that by building a dataset of 20,000 human proteins with both their 3D structures and where they actually go in the cell.

problem.h2: The missing piece in protein prediction
paras: Predicting where a protein goes in a cell matters for finding drug targets and understanding what a protein does. For decades, biologists did this by hand in the lab, which is slow and expensive.

When machine learning showed up, researchers built a shortcut: given just the sequence of amino acids (the genetic text), predict the location. One benchmark, DeepLoc, contains protein sequences and location labels but nothing else. The problem is that a protein's shape dictates how it behaves and where it ends up in the cell, yet DeepLoc never shows the model any shape information at all.

callout.html: The dataset only has sequences, not the 3D protein shapes that determine where a protein actually goes.

panels.title: 1. The old way: sequence alone
panels.viz_args: GAVLIMFPSTCNQEDKRHYW...GAVLIMFPST (just a text string of amino acids)
panels.caption: Old dataset: 20,000 proteins, each just a long text sequence, no shape info.

panels.title: 2. What the model misses
panels.caption: Shape buried inside the sequence. Model cannot see it, so it guesses poorly.

panels.title: 3. CAPSUL adds the shape
panels.caption: For each protein, add the 3D structure from AlphaFold2: where atoms sit, how they connect.

panels.title: 4. Three ways to encode shape
panels.viz_args: Graph (bonds/contacts) or Tokens (structural fingerprint) or Coordinate (geometry)
panels.caption: CAPSUL gives three shape encodings; models can pick which one helps most.

panels.title: 5. Shape predicts location better
panels.caption: Adding shape pushes accuracy higher for models that know how to use it.

steps.text: Grab 20,504 human protein structures from AlphaFold2 (a tool that predicts 3D shape from sequence).
Domain experts label each protein: does it go to the nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, etc.? Twenty compartments total.
For each protein, represent its shape as a graph (bonds), tokens (fingerprints), or raw coordinates.
Run both sequence-only and structure-aware models; measure which learn location better because structure lets the model see the real physical clues cells use.

When structure helps, look at which parts of the shape the model focused on because high attention means the model learned that part predicts location. Found alpha-helix regions drive Golgi targeting.

paras: The paper adds 3D protein structure data to the benchmark, alongside the sequence and location label. Where the old dataset was just (sequence, location), the new one is (sequence, 3D structure in three forms, location).

hidden.name: How much each part of the shape matters for location
paras: A protein is a 3D folded chain; each atom has a position in 3D space. When a model reads the shape via attention (a neural mechanism that learns to focus on important parts), it assigns a weight to each amino acid residue: high weight means this part determines the location prediction. The paper extracts these attention weights after training to see which structural patterns predict localization.

The paper measures this by training a graph model (like a network that treats the protein as a connected graph) with added Transformer layers (a module designed to focus on the most important pieces). It then reads off which residues got the highest attention scores, revealing the structural pattern the model discovered.

heat.caption: Darker means the model paid more attention to this part. Highlighted residues form an alpha-helix driving Golgi localization.

reads.html: Some parts of a protein's shape are decisive for its location. Attention weights tell us which ones.
The Transformer encoder assigns attention weights to residues; high-attention residues form interpretable structural patterns like alpha-helices.

paras: A protein sequence is a 1D string, but the protein folds into a specific 3D shape. That shape determines what the protein bumps into, where it sticks, and how the cell recognizes it. The cell's machinery reads the shape to sort proteins to the right place.

Models trained on sequence alone must guess the shape from the text. Models trained on both sequence and structure see the real shape directly, so they learn faster and more accurately. Because the model can now see how atoms are arranged—which atoms are close, which parts stick out, which regions are tight or loose—it learns which structural features predict each location. The paper shows that when you add a Transformer layer to a graph encoder, the model learns to focus on the most decisive structural parts (like alpha-helix regions for Golgi), which matches what biologists already know and opens a path to discover new patterns.

stages.s: Encode 3D structure as graph or tokens
Transformer layer focuses on critical residues
Predict location; read which parts mattered most

math.h2: The loss function for focal and contrastive learning
math.words: loss_total = focal_loss + lambda * contrastive_loss, where focal_loss weights hard-to-classify locations more heavily and contrastive_loss pulls together proteins that go to the same place
math.equation: L = w_focal * L_focal(y, pred) + lambda * L_contrastive(pos_pairs, neg_pairs)
symbols: weight from focal loss, higher for rare or hard locations
focal loss: penalizes wrong predictions more when the location is rare
mixing weight, how much contrastive learning helps overall
pulls proteins to same location closer together, pushes different locations apart

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a protein should go to the nucleus (location A). The model says 'Golgi' (location B) with 60% confidence.
Focal loss spot-check: if the nucleus is common (w_focal = 1.0) and the model is wrong, penalty is 1.0 * large_value = large.
If the nucleus is rare (w_focal = 3.0), same wrong prediction gets 3.0 * large_value = 3x worse penalty.
Contrastive loss: pair this nucleus protein with 10 other nucleus proteins; push their number lists closer together. Penalty shrinks as they cluster.
Pair a nucleus protein with a Golgi protein; pull them apart. Penalty grows if they stay close.
Total: L = 3.0 * 0.8 + 0.2 * 0.15 = 2.4 + 0.03 = 2.43. Focal term dominates because the nucleus is rare.

math.note: Focal loss makes the model try harder on rare locations; contrastive loss naturally separates proteins by location in the number-list space, so the classifier gets cleaner clusters to work with.

bars.h2: Sequence alone versus sequence plus structure

charts.title: Sequence-only model (no structure)
charts.note: Model guesses structure from text. Rare locations are especially hard.

charts.title: This paper: sequence + 3D shape
charts.note: Model sees real shape. All locations improve, especially rare ones where structure clues matter most because structure provides physical signals that override sequence ambiguity.

items.html: The 3D shapes come from AlphaFold2, which predicts structure from sequence. If the prediction is poor, the model trains on wrong atomic positions. The paper does not validate all structures against real experiments.

Focal loss helps but does not fully fix the core problem because if only 5% of proteins go to the nucleus, the model gets 95 examples of other locations for every 5 nucleus examples—the sheer volume of wrong-place examples drowns out the signal. Contrastive loss helps by clustering, but focal weights alone cannot overcome this severe class imbalance because the problem is not penalty size but data volume.

items.b: Attention patterns may not be causal.
items.html: When the model pays attention to alpha-helices, it might mean alpha-helices drive localization, or it might mean alpha-helices happen to be nearby and correlate with the real signal. The paper shows correlation, not proof of causation.
When structure is included, experts validate a sample of predictions. The paper does a case study on Golgi and confirms that the discovered alpha-helix pattern matches known biology.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train two models on a mini version of CAPSUL: one takes only sequence, one takes sequence plus a simplified 3D encoding (e.g., distance between each pair of residues). On a held-out test set of 500 proteins across all 20 locations, measure accuracy and F1-score. Plot both metrics as bars, and for the structure-aware model, extract and visualize the top 10 highest-attention residues for one example protein. Show that structure-aware predictions are more accurate because the model can see physical clues, and that attention highlights a known structural motif because the model learned to focus on shape features that biologists know matter.
demo.closing: The structure-aware model learns to recognize biological features and make fewer mistakes, especially on rare locations.
